name: Pricing Into the Habit: When Inelastic Demand Is the Business Model
deck: Where demand is structurally inelastic because of addiction, chronic disease, or regulatory lock-in, companies raise prices independent of volume trends and shareholders reward the pricing discipline.
core_bet: Companies that control inelastic demand—whether through addictive products, chronic-disease management, or institutional medical necessity—have discovered that they can grow earnings by raising prices even when volumes are flat or declining. This is not a business insight; it is a cash-harvest strategy where the customer has no choice and the company has no reason to invest in growth. Philip Morris grew combustibles revenues 9.5% while volumes declined; BrightSpring raised revenue per prescription to $314.20 on flat script counts. The habit, not innovation, is the pricing engine.

mechanism: Inelastic demand has a precise economic meaning: quantity demanded does not change meaningfully when price rises because consumers cannot switch, have no alternatives, or face severe penalties for non-use. In pharmaceuticals, nicotine, and chronic-care management, this elasticity is close to zero. A diabetic patient cannot choose to stop using insulin when the price rises 20%. A nicotine-dependent person cannot simply walk away when cigarettes cost more. A post-acute-care patient cannot refuse pharmacy services when reimbursement rates increase. This is where the cash harvest begins. Once a company controls an inelastic-demand channel, pricing power becomes disconnected from operational improvement, innovation, or value creation. The customer pays more because they have no choice, not because they are receiving something better.

Philip Morris International demonstrates the model in its purest form. In Q2 2026, the company grew combustibles net revenues 9.5% while shipment volumes actually declined. This is not a story about winning market share or growing the smoking population. It is a story about extracting more cash from an existing, shrinking base of addicted customers. The company still has 43 million people using its smoke-free products, down slightly, but revenues are up. The mechanism is simple: raise prices. Because nicotine addiction is one of the most inelastic demand systems on earth, customers absorb the price increase. Management does not have to invest in innovation, marketing, or product development. It just has to change the price list. EPS jumped from $4.52 to $7.26 in a single year not because Philip Morris made better cigarettes. It is because the company realized it could extract substantially more cash from existing customers.

BrightSpring's pharmacy model shows the same pattern in healthcare. The company's Q2 2026 results show prescriptions dispensed were 'broadly stable'—flat volumes—while revenue per script rose to $314.20 and gross profit per script rose to $27.50. BrightSpring fulfilled approximately 43 million prescriptions in 2025, and that base is not growing. But the company is making more money from it. The driver is not better service or more valuable medication. It is the ability to raise prices on a captive population of chronic-disease patients who have no choice but to take their medications. A cancer patient on specialty pharmacy cannot call a competitor. A dialysis patient cannot switch providers on a whim. A home-health patient cannot refuse to have their nurse visits managed. These are medically dependent populations, and BrightSpring controls the infrastructure. Price power comes with that control.
why_now: Three forces have aligned to make the addiction-pricing engine visible now. First, the secular decline in growth has made investors desperate for any source of earnings that does not require reinvestment in capacity or innovation. Inelastic-demand businesses deliver growth without capex: just raise prices. Second, healthcare consolidation has made chronic-disease and specialty-pharmacy management increasingly concentrated in a few large platforms (BrightSpring, CVS, Cigna). As the industry consolidates, individual companies have less competitive pressure to compete on price and more ability to set terms. Third, nicotine categories have stopped declining and stabilized at a lower level. Philip Morris no longer has to fight daily decline; it can now harvest from a stable base. That stability makes the pricing strategy sustainable. The addiction is permanent, the customer base is known, and the elasticity is zero. Therefore, price increases can flow directly to earnings.
who_pays: Concrete people pay in specific ways. Smokers pay more money per cigarette—a pack that cost $8 five years ago costs $12 today. A patient on a specialty pharmaceutical might be trapped in a $5,000-per-month therapy where the insurance company or patient pays, then the pharmacy's rebate structure means the patient's copay rises annually even though the underlying drug did not improve. A cancer patient on an infusion therapy managed by BrightSpring pays through their insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs as the company raises revenue per script. A family managing a loved one in home health pays through insurance and through reduced access to other services as consolidated providers like BrightSpring raise prices faster than underlying inflation. The burden falls hardest on the patients and families with the least ability to absorb price increases: low-income smokers, chronic-disease populations with limited alternatives, and families managing elder care or end-of-life services.
who_profits: Four groups profit directly. First, the companies themselves: Philip Morris, BrightSpring, Cigna, Cencora, and McKesson all report strong earnings growth tied to price increases on inelastic demand. Second, the shareholders of those companies who receive buybacks and dividend growth funded by cash harvested from price increases. Third, the financial sponsors and private-equity firms that have backed companies like BrightSpring, understanding that chronic-disease management is a low-growth, high-margin, price-disciplined business. Fourth, financial intermediaries like Cigna and CVS that control both the supply side (as a pharmacy benefit manager or pharmacy operator) and demand side (as an insurer), allowing them to keep more of the rent at every step. The profit pool has narrowed and concentrated.
tension: The breaking point comes when price increases hit absolute affordability walls or when regulation intervenes. Philip Morris faces this in territories where excise taxes are already high and cigarette prices approach true luxury levels for working-class consumers. BrightSpring faces it when state Medicaid programs, which pay a large share of home health and specialty pharmacy costs, simply refuse to pay higher rates and providers lose volume. Cigna and Cencora face it when employers and government programs push back against pharmaceutical inflation and specialty-drug pricing. At some threshold, the inelastic-demand assumption breaks. When a patient cannot afford both their medication and food, when a family chooses to skip doses to stretch prescriptions, when a state legislature passes drug-pricing controls, the pricing engine stalls. The other tension is that inelastic demand attracts regulatory attention. Nicotine pricing has become a political issue; healthcare pricing is under constant legislative threat. Companies are harvesting from this demand precisely because they know regulators and competitors cannot touch it. But that premium on 'untouchable' demand is exactly what makes regulators eventually touch it.
surprising_part: The surprise is not that companies raise prices—that is forecastable. The surprise is how nakedly the financial community rewards this strategy even when volume is falling. Philip Morris's EPS jumped 60% on declining cigarette volumes. That should be a scandal, but it is celebrated as 'pricing discipline' and 'margin expansion'. BrightSpring raised revenue per script on flat volumes and the market applauded it as 'optimization' and 'operating leverage'. The second surprise is how little reinvestment these businesses require. Philip Morris does not need to build factories or develop new products; it just changes prices. BrightSpring does not need to hire more clinicians or improve care; it just raises the price per script. This is the most efficient possible business: harvesting existing demand without investing anything. That efficiency is exactly what makes it unsustainable, because eventually somebody notices that no value is being created, only redistributed.
one_sentence: When demand is truly addictive or medically necessary, companies stop innovating and start harvesting—raising prices on captive customers and pocketing the margin until regulation or affordability breaks the model.
societal_stake: This is how inequality gets systematized into healthcare and consumer products. The people most addicted to nicotine are low-income smokers who cannot quit; they pay ever-higher prices. The people most dependent on chronic-disease medications are sicker, poorer populations without negotiating power; they pay more. The people most vulnerable to home-health and specialty-pharmacy pricing are the elderly and disabled who have no alternatives. The pricing engine extracts value specifically from the most vulnerable populations because those populations have the least elasticity—they have to pay or die. The business model works perfectly as long as the victims have no voice. But when a political movement or regulatory authority decides that addiction pricing is unjust, the entire financial structure collapses because the economics depend on captive demand having no choice.
